transcript.text: Price Floors
GENERAL ECONOMICS
GEN-ECON-20
Time: 5 minutes
Outcome: Distinguish binding and nonbinding floors and analyze surpluses and unintended effects.
Difficulty: Beginner
THE CORE IDEA

A price floor sets a legal minimum price and is binding only when it lies above the market equilibrium price. A binding floor keeps price from falling to equilibrium, so quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded and a surplus develops. A floor at or below equilibrium is nonbinding because the market can still reach its equilibrium price.
HOW TO RECOGNIZE IT
Compare the legal minimum price with the market equilibrium price.
A floor above equilibrium is binding and creates excess supply.
At the floor price, read quantity supplied and quantity demanded; their difference is the surplus.
A floor at or below equilibrium is nonbinding and does not change the market outcome.
WATCH OUT
A common mistake is to assume that every price floor is binding. Equilibrium is $30. A floor at $20 is below equilibrium, so it does not prevent the market from reaching $30.
WORKED EXAMPLE: BINDING PRICE FLOOR

The horizontal axis is quantity and the vertical axis is price. An upward-sloping supply curve and downward-sloping demand curve intersect at price $30 and quantity 200. Dashed guides also show demand and supply quantities at prices $10, $20, $40, and $50: at $10, supply is 100 and demand is 300; at $20, supply is 150 and demand is 250; at $40, supply is 250 and demand is 150; at $50, supply is 300 and demand is 100.

The market equilibrium is $30 and 200 units. A binding floor of $40 holds price above equilibrium; sellers offer 250 units while buyers demand 150. The resulting surplus is 250 - 150 = 100 units, so some output remains unsold at the controlled price.
CHECK YOURSELF
At a binding price floor, Qs = 110 and Qd = 80. What is the surplus?
